Each is a single closed loop in which every node has exactly two neighbors." width="100%"} Creates n nodes in a circular pattern where the last connects back to first. Each node has exactly degree `2`. A cycle graph (often written C_n) is a path of `n` nodes plus one extra edge closing the loop, so it has `n` nodes and `n` edges. Every node plays the same role, which means centrality measures give all nodes the same score, and removing any single edge leaves a connected path. Cycles are useful for: - testing algorithms that detect cycles, bipartiteness (even `n` is bipartite, odd `n` is not), or girth - modelling ring-shaped structures like ring networks, circular routes, or round-robin schedules - serving as a symmetric baseline when comparing centrality or clustering results Nodes are labelled exactly as in `add_path_graph()`: each with its node ID as a string (`"1"` to `"n"` in an empty graph). In a directed graph the edges run `1 -> 2 -> ... -> n -> 1`, forming a directed cycle. The cycle is added as a new, separate component, the graph is modified in place, and the construction is recorded as a single step in the step log (see `steps`). ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [n]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Number of nodes in the cycle (minimum `3`, the triangle). The cycle will also have `n` edges. [type]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional node type/category assigned to all new nodes (stored in the `type` column of the node DataFrame). Default is `None`, which leaves the type unset. [label]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), label each node with its ID as described above (a label that is already used raises `ValueError` before anything is added). If `False`, the nodes are left unlabelled. [rel]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Optional[str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional relationship label assigned to all edges of the cycle, including the closing edge (stored in the `rel` column of the edge DataFrame). Default is `None`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `n=` is less than `3`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle graph is a path graph with one extra edge closing the loop back to the start, so it has as many edges as it has nodes: ::: {#f9be19d7 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=4) graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (4, 4) ``` ::: ::: Every node has exactly two neighbors. A cycle with an even number of nodes is bipartite, while an odd one is not: ::: {#7fa6c909 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph.get_node_df()["degree"].to_list(), graph.is_bipartite(), ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(n=5).is_bipartite(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([2, 2, 2, 2], True, False) ``` ::: ::: In a directed graph the edges follow one direction around the ring, with the last edge (here `4 -> 1`) closing the loop. `rel=` applies to every edge: ::: {#687772fa .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ring = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_cycle_graph(n=4, rel="next") ring.get_edge_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
